title: DPI Ecosystem Overview
subtitle: Understanding the Global Landscape
description: Understand the global DPI ecosystem including key players, platforms, and standards.
targetAudience: DPI advisors, government IT directors, policy coordinators

content.overview: DPI (Digital Public Infrastructure) is a foundational approach to digital development that enables government services, economic opportunity, and social benefit through interoperable digital systems. This module defines DPI, distinguishes it from broader digital transformation, and establishes the core concepts that underpin the entire ecosystem.

keyPoints.title: Definition and Scope
keyPoints.description: DPI encompasses foundational digital systems that governments and markets can build upon. It includes digital identity systems, payment infrastructure, and data exchange protocols that serve as the backbone for both public services and economic activity.
keyPoints.example: India's Aadhaar digital identity has enabled over 1.4 billion biometric registrations, serving as the foundation for benefits delivery and financial inclusion across multiple sectors.

keyPoints.title: Core Pillars
keyPoints.description: DPI is built on three essential pillars: digital identity for authentication and rights verification, payment systems for secure value transfer, and data sharing infrastructure for interoperable information exchange.
keyPoints.example: Singapore's National Digital Identity framework integrates SingPass (authentication), PayNow (payment), and MyInfo (data sharing) to create a seamless ecosystem for both citizen services and business transactions.

keyPoints.title: Distinction from Digital Transformation
keyPoints.description: While digital transformation modernizes specific services, DPI provides the underlying infrastructure that multiple services and sectors can leverage, creating network effects and reducing duplication.
keyPoints.example: Rwanda's digital strategy focuses on building foundational DPI systems first—mobile money through MTN Mobile Money, digital ID through NIDA—before expanding specific service digitization.

keyPoints.title: Public Good Nature
keyPoints.description: DPI systems are designed as public goods or regulated utilities that follow open standards, ensuring equal access and reducing monopolistic control of critical infrastructure.
keyPoints.example: The EU's digital wallet initiative mandates open standards and interoperability requirements, preventing vendor lock-in and ensuring citizens maintain control of their digital credentials.

keyPoints.title: Interoperability as Core Principle
keyPoints.description: DPI succeeds through interoperability—the ability of different systems and services to work together seamlessly. This requires open standards, clear APIs, and governance frameworks.
keyPoints.example: Brazil's Central Bank Open Banking Framework mandates that financial institutions share customer data and payment capabilities through standardized APIs, enabling fintech innovation across the ecosystem.

content.keyInsight: DPI is not about building specific applications, but creating the foundational infrastructure layer that enables governments, businesses, and citizens to participate in digital ecosystems with trust, security, and efficiency. It's the digital equivalent of roads, electricity, and telephone networks that enabled twentieth-century development.

exercises.prompt: Reflect on your country's or region's approach to digital services. What foundational infrastructure exists today? What gaps prevent seamless digital participation?
Compare two countries' digital strategies. Which elements are foundational DPI versus specific service applications? What's the relationship between the two?

content.overview: The global DPI landscape is rapidly evolving, with significant variation in maturity, approach, and success across regions. This module maps the current state of DPI implementation worldwide, identifies regional patterns, and explores how different countries have adapted DPI principles to their unique contexts.

keyPoints.title: Maturity Levels
keyPoints.description: Countries exhibit varying levels of DPI maturity, from nascent systems in early-stage implementations to sophisticated, multi-layered ecosystems with strong integration across sectors.
keyPoints.example: Estonia has achieved advanced DPI maturity with X-Road (data exchange), e-ID (digital identity), and blockchain-based governance, while many Sub-Saharan African nations are building foundational digital identity systems as their first DPI component.

keyPoints.title: Regional Patterns
keyPoints.description: Different regions show distinct patterns in DPI adoption based on historical context, economic development, governance capacity, and specific challenges. Asia, Africa, and Latin America have developed region-specific DPI models.
keyPoints.example: East Africa's regional cooperation through the East African Community has facilitated cross-border DPI standards for digital identity and payments, while Southeast Asia through ASEAN is developing interregional payment rails.

keyPoints.title: Development Stage Classification
keyPoints.description: Countries can be classified into stages: planning and pilot, foundational (identity/payments), intermediate (data sharing), and advanced (integrated ecosystem). Understanding these stages helps identify peer countries.
keyPoints.example: India is in the advanced stage with integrated Aadhaar-UPI-GSTN ecosystem; Kenya is intermediate with Huduma Number and M-Pesa integration; and several post-conflict states are in foundational stage.

keyPoints.title: Global DPI Leaders
keyPoints.description: Leading DPI ecosystems include Estonia, Singapore, India, UAE, Colombia, and South Korea. Each provides lessons in design, governance, and implementation approaches suited to their context.
keyPoints.example: Colombia's Sistema de Identificación Integral (SIID) combined with the digital financial ecosystem through fintech regulations created an inclusive DPI model adapted to a developing economy context.

keyPoints.title: Emerging Implementation Models
keyPoints.description: New models are emerging including decentralized identity approaches, blockchain-based infrastructure, mobile-first designs for developing markets, and public-private partnership governance models.
keyPoints.example: El Salvador's implementation of Bitcoin as legal tender alongside digital identity initiatives represents an emerging, unconventional DPI approach leveraging cryptocurrency infrastructure.

content.keyInsight: There is no single 'right' DPI model. Success depends on aligning DPI principles with country context—governance capacity, economic needs, technical infrastructure, and institutional maturity. Learning from global examples helps identify relevant solutions, but each country must design its own path.

exercises.prompt: Create a maturity assessment for your country across three DPI pillars: digital identity, payments, and data sharing. Place your country on the development stage spectrum.
Select one leading DPI ecosystem and one emerging ecosystem at your country's development stage. Compare their approaches, governance models, and timelines. What lessons apply to your context?

content.overview: Effective DPI ecosystems are built on interconnected building blocks that work together to enable digital participation. This module explores the core components of DPI systems, their functions, interactions, and critical success factors for each component.

keyPoints.title: Digital Identity
keyPoints.description: Digital identity systems create a verified, unique digital representation of individuals, enabling authentication and authorization across services. Modern systems use biometrics, credentials, and cryptographic protocols.
keyPoints.example: India's Aadhaar employs 10-point iris biometrics and fingerprinting to create unique IDs for 1.4+ billion residents. It serves as the foundation for direct benefit transfers, KYC verification, and tax administration—demonstrating how digital identity becomes the key that unlocks other services.

keyPoints.title: Payment and Settlement Systems
keyPoints.description: Real-time, interoperable payment infrastructure enables secure value transfer. This includes immediate payment systems (like India's UPI), blockchain-based settlement, and digital currency infrastructure.
keyPoints.example: India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processes 8+ billion transactions monthly across 300+ partner banks through a standardized API layer, enabling mobile money, QR-based payments, and recurring transactions at near-zero marginal cost.

keyPoints.title: Data Exchange Infrastructure
keyPoints.description: Secure, consent-based data sharing platforms enable services to access verified information without duplication. These use APIs, service directories, and governance frameworks to manage data flow.
keyPoints.example: Estonia's X-Road is a secure data exchange layer connecting 1,000+ organizations, enabling government services to access citizen data once without re-requesting. It uses strong encryption, audit trails, and citizen consent logging.

keyPoints.title: Digital Credentials and Attestations
keyPoints.description: Verifiable, portable digital credentials replace physical documents. These include educational credentials, professional licenses, and capability attestations that citizens can share selectively.
keyPoints.example: The EU's eIDAS regulation enables digital signatures and seals with legal equivalence to handwritten signatures. Countries like Germany and Portugal issue digital professional licenses and educational credentials with blockchain verification.

keyPoints.title: Service Directories and Catalogs
keyPoints.description: Standardized catalogs of available services and their APIs help service providers and users discover, integrate, and optimize services across the ecosystem.
keyPoints.example: Singapore's GovTech service catalog lists all digital services, their APIs, and integration requirements, enabling private sector developers to build services that integrate with government systems through standardized endpoints.

keyPoints.title: Governance and Standards Bodies
keyPoints.description: Formal institutions manage standards development, security compliance, data protection, and dispute resolution. These ensure alignment without centralizing control.
keyPoints.example: India's MEITY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) sets standards for Aadhaar authentication while NPCI manages the UPI ecosystem, allowing both regulatory oversight and ecosystem innovation.

content.keyInsight: No single building block operates in isolation. Digital identity gains value when connected to payments; payments drive inclusive commerce when based on universal digital identity; data sharing creates efficiency when identity and payments provide the foundation. Design for systemic integration, not component optimization.

exercises.prompt: Map your country's DPI components across the six building blocks. Which are mature? Which are nascent? What are the interconnections and gaps?
Design a DPI roadmap sequence for a developing country starting from scratch. In what order should components be built? Why? What are the dependencies?

content.overview: Global DPI development relies on established platforms, protocols, and standards that enable interoperability and reduce reinvention. This module surveys major platforms, standards bodies, and frameworks that countries use when building or integrating DPI systems.

keyPoints.title: Foundational Standards
keyPoints.description: International standards provide common ground for DPI components. Key standards include ISO/IEC for identity verification, NIST standards for cybersecurity, and ITU-T recommendations for telecommunications.
keyPoints.example: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is used globally—from Singapore to Rwanda—to establish baseline security requirements for DPI systems. ISO/IEC 27001 provides identity and access management standards adopted across government DPI implementations.

keyPoints.title: Identity Standards
keyPoints.description: Standards for digital identity include W3C's DID (Decentralized Identifiers), OpenID Connect for authentication, SAML for federation, and national standards like India's Aadhaar-based verification protocols.
keyPoints.example: The W3C's Verifiable Credentials standard is gaining adoption in EU member states, India, and developing economies as a portable, interoperable credential format that users can carry across systems.

keyPoints.title: Payment Standards
keyPoints.description: Payment infrastructure standards include ISO 20022 for financial messaging, payment network rules from VISA/Mastercard, and emerging blockchain standards like Ethereum for DeFi applications.
keyPoints.example: Brazil's Open Banking Framework uses ISO 20022 standard messages, enabling fintech companies to compete with traditional banks while maintaining standardized data formats and interoperability.

keyPoints.title: Data Exchange Protocols
keyPoints.description: Protocols for secure data sharing include REST APIs with OpenAPI specifications, GraphQL for flexible queries, and emerging standards like IndieAuth for decentralized authentication.
keyPoints.example: Estonia's X-Road uses REST APIs with comprehensive logging and encryption, enabling secure data exchange. The standard is now being adopted by other European countries through the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure.

keyPoints.title: Open-Source DPI Platforms
keyPoints.description: Several open-source platforms enable countries to build DPI systems without proprietary dependencies. These include Mosip (identity), OpenIMIS (health insurance), and Mifos X (financial inclusion).
keyPoints.example: MOSIP (Modular Open Source Identity Platform) is used by 10+ countries including India, Kenya, and Bangladesh. It provides modular identity components—biometric capture, registration, authentication—that countries can customize.

keyPoints.title: Governance and Compliance Standards
keyPoints.description: Standards like GDPR (EU), Kenya's Data Protection Act, and India's consent-based data sharing frameworks establish governance requirements that DPI systems must meet.
keyPoints.example: The GDPR's requirements for data minimization and user consent influenced India's non-personal data framework and inform emerging DPI governance standards across Africa and Latin America.

content.keyInsight: Using established standards accelerates implementation, improves security, and enables international interoperability. However, standards alone don't determine success—local adaptation, strong governance implementation, and ecosystem coordination are equally critical. Choose standards that align with your governance model and technical capacity.

exercises.prompt: Audit your country's DPI implementations against international standards. Which standards are followed? Which are missing? What's the impact of gaps?
You're tasked with building a national digital identity system. Compare MOSIP, proprietary solutions, and custom development approaches. What would you recommend for your country's context and why?

content.overview: The global DPI ecosystem is enabled by multilateral organizations, technical communities, and peer networks that facilitate knowledge sharing, standard-setting, and collective problem-solving. This module maps the key actors that drive DPI development globally.

keyPoints.title: Multilateral Development Banks
keyPoints.description: The World Bank, ADB, AfDB, and IDB provide financing, technical assistance, and convening power for DPI initiatives. They establish frameworks like the World Bank's ID4D (Identification for Development) initiative.
keyPoints.example: The World Bank's ID4D initiative has financed digital identity systems in 50+ countries, establishing the universal DPI principle that governments should provide foundational identity before vertical applications.

keyPoints.title: UN and Specialized Agencies
keyPoints.description: UNCDF, UNECA, and other UN agencies promote DPI adoption aligned with SDGs. UNECA leads African digital transformation agenda; UNCDF focuses on financial inclusion through DPI.
keyPoints.example: UNCDF's Digital Finance Inclusion Initiative in Sub-Saharan Africa promotes DPI-enabled financial services, linking digital identity to savings accounts and insurance products across 16 countries.

keyPoints.title: Regional Organizations
keyPoints.description: ASEAN, African Union, Pacific Islands Forum, and other regional bodies coordinate DPI standards and facilitate cross-border DPI integration within their regions.
keyPoints.example: ASEAN's Digital Economy Framework Work Plan includes standardized APIs for cross-border payment, digital identity recognition, and e-commerce, enabling DPI interoperability across Southeast Asia.

keyPoints.title: Technical Communities and Standards Bodies
keyPoints.description: W3C, IETF, ISO, and IEC develop and maintain technical standards. Communities like Linux Foundation and OpenStack provide open-source infrastructure for DPI systems.
keyPoints.example: The Linux Foundation's Hyperledger Fabric is used in DPI implementations from India to Kenya for secure data sharing and credential verification, providing community-supported infrastructure.

keyPoints.title: Country Networks and Peer Learning
keyPoints.description: Countries increasingly share DPI experience through bilateral programs, regional workshops, and global forums. India-Africa partnerships, ASEAN peer learning, and Caribbean cooperation groups accelerate DPI adoption.
keyPoints.example: India's DPI leadership model has catalyzed peer learning networks where countries like Kenya, Bangladesh, and Nigeria send delegations to learn from Aadhaar-UPI-GSTN integration.

keyPoints.title: Private Sector and Ecosystem Partners
keyPoints.description: Technology companies, fintech firms, and civil society organizations build on DPI foundations. Private sector engagement through hackathons, innovation programs, and partner ecosystems amplifies DPI impact.
keyPoints.example: India's UPI success is enabled by 300+ partner banks and 15,000+ fintech startups building on the open API, creating a competitive ecosystem rather than a monopoly platform.

content.keyInsight: No single organization drives DPI development. Success requires coordination among development banks for financing, UN agencies for normative guidance, technical communities for standards, and country networks for peer learning. Effective DPI governance bridges these different actors while maintaining sovereign country control over implementation.

exercises.prompt: Map the key organizations, networks, and actors involved in DPI development in your region. Identify critical relationships and gaps in the ecosystem.
Develop a partnership strategy for your country's DPI development. Which multilateral organizations, regional bodies, and peer networks should be engaged? What are the negotiation priorities?

content.overview: Examining successful DPI implementations across different country contexts reveals how principles are adapted to local conditions. This module provides detailed case studies of leading DPI ecosystems, analyzing their trajectories, design decisions, and outcomes.

keyPoints.title: India: Digital Identity as DPI Foundation
keyPoints.description: India's Aadhaar (digital identity with 1.4+ billion registrations) serves as the foundation for UPI (8+ billion monthly payment transactions) and GSTIN (20+ million businesses registered). This integrated ecosystem demonstrates how digital identity creates network effects across payments, taxation, and services.
keyPoints.example: A small farmer in rural Rajasthan with an Aadhaar ID can open a bank account (using eKYC), access agricultural credit (through digital verification), receive government subsidies (via direct benefit transfers), and sell produce through agricultural supply chain platforms—all enabled by the foundational Aadhaar system.

keyPoints.title: Estonia: DPI as State Modernization Strategy
keyPoints.description: Estonia's X-Road (data exchange), e-ID (digital identity), and blockchain governance created a 'digital state' where 99% of public services are digital, with citizens accessing services through a single digital entrance.
keyPoints.example: Estonian citizens can incorporate a company in 15 minutes, file taxes in 10 minutes, and access all government services through a single digital portal. The government reduced back-office costs by 30% while improving service quality through DPI-enabled digitization.

keyPoints.title: Singapore: DPI as Economic Competitiveness Strategy
keyPoints.description: Singapore's smart nation strategy integrated SingPass (digital identity), PayNow (real-time payments), and MyInfo (verified data) into a comprehensive ecosystem connecting government, businesses, and citizens.
keyPoints.example: A Singapore resident can open a business bank account using SingPass, verify credentials through MyInfo, access government grants through one portal, and process payments through PayNow—all within a single integrated ecosystem.

keyPoints.title: Colombia: DPI in Middle-Income Context
keyPoints.description: Colombia built a comprehensive DPI system including SIID (digital identity), PQRD (single public complaint system), and integrated fintech regulations that enabled financial inclusion despite institutional constraints.
keyPoints.example: Colombia's digital identity system combined with open fintech regulations enabled companies like Rappi and Nubank to offer financial services to previously unbanked populations, creating economic inclusion through DPI.

keyPoints.title: Kenya: DPI as Financial Inclusion Accelerator
keyPoints.description: Kenya's Huduma Number (digital identity), M-Pesa (mobile money), and emerging digital service platforms demonstrate how DPI can work in lower-income contexts with significant informal economies.
keyPoints.example: Kenya's M-Pesa ecosystem processes 50+ billion USD annually, enabling cash-less transactions across informal economies. The system works because it's built on accessible infrastructure (USSD on basic phones) and trust in Safaricom's stability.

keyPoints.title: United Arab Emirates: DPI as Governance Digitization
keyPoints.description: UAE's Emirates ID (digital identity), blockchain-based contract verification, and integrated government services demonstrated how DPI can support rapid government modernization in an oil-rich context.
keyPoints.example: The UAE's paperless government initiative enabled all government services to operate digitally, reducing processing times and improving transparency through blockchain-recorded transactions and digital ID verification.

content.keyInsight: These case studies reveal that DPI success depends less on technology choice and more on governance clarity, sustained investment, regulatory alignment, and ecosystem coordination. Each country adapted DPI principles to its unique context—but all shared a focus on foundational infrastructure before vertical applications.

exercises.prompt: Select two case studies with similar development contexts (e.g., India and Kenya, Estonia and Singapore). Compare their DPI approaches, timelines, and outcomes. What explains the differences in implementation strategy?
Choose the case study most similar to your country's context. Identify 3-5 elements you could adapt directly and 3-5 elements you would need to modify. Explain why.

content.overview: The DPI landscape is evolving rapidly with new technologies, governance models, and use cases emerging. This module explores emerging trends that will shape DPI development over the next 5-10 years.

keyPoints.title: Decentralized and User-Centric Identity
keyPoints.description: Moving from centralized government-issued identity to user-controlled, decentralized identities using blockchain and cryptographic standards (W3C DIDs). This gives citizens control over which attributes they share.
keyPoints.example: The EU's digital wallet initiatives are piloting W3C Verifiable Credentials, enabling citizens to carry portable, cryptographically verified credentials—from education to professional qualifications—that they control and share selectively.

keyPoints.title: Blockchain and Distributed Ledger Technology
keyPoints.description: Using blockchain for immutable credential verification, smart contracts for automated service delivery, and distributed governance. However, blockchain alone does not solve DPI challenges; it's a tool, not a solution.
keyPoints.example: Estonia is exploring blockchain-based credentials for government data exchanges. India is experimenting with blockchain-based health credentials (CoWIN vaccination records) and land registries.

keyPoints.title: Privacy-Preserving Technologies
keyPoints.description: Advancing cryptographic techniques—differential privacy, zero-knowledge proofs, and homomorphic encryption—that enable data analysis and verification without exposing sensitive individual data.
keyPoints.example: The UK's trusted research environments use privacy-preserving techniques to enable health researchers to analyze NHS data without accessing individual records, enabling innovation while protecting privacy.

keyPoints.title: Cross-Border DPI Integration
keyPoints.description: Enabling citizens to use digital identity and payment systems across borders. This requires interoperability agreements, mutual recognition frameworks, and standardized credential formats.
keyPoints.example: ASEAN's digital economy framework includes agreements for mutual recognition of digital identity and payments, enabling ASEAN citizens to participate in cross-border services, remittances, and commerce.

keyPoints.title: AI and Intelligent Service Delivery
keyPoints.description: Using AI to personalize service recommendations, predict eligibility for government programs, and automate service delivery based on verified identity and credentials.
keyPoints.example: Singapore and Estonia are piloting AI-powered government service recommendations that predict what services citizens may need based on their verified profile (new parent? = childcare benefits) without users manually searching.

keyPoints.title: Mobile-First and Offline-First Architectures
keyPoints.description: Designing DPI systems for connectivity constraints in developing markets, using technologies like USSD, offline capability, and edge computing.
keyPoints.example: Kenya's M-Pesa works over USSD (available on basic phones), enabling financial services for unconnected populations. This model is being replicated in rural India, Pakistan, and Sub-Saharan Africa.

content.keyInsight: Emerging technologies offer new possibilities for DPI—but they're solutions to specific problems, not replacements for foundational principles. Decentralized identity, blockchain, and AI are valuable when they solve real constraints; they're expensive failures when implemented for their own sake. Evaluate emerging trends against your country's specific challenges and capacities.

exercises.prompt: Select two emerging trends most relevant to your country's context. Analyze how each could address current DPI challenges or limitations. What are the implementation requirements and risks?
Develop a 5-year scenario for how one emerging trend (e.g., decentralized identity, cross-border DPI integration) could reshape your country's digital ecosystem. What are the opportunities and risks?

content.overview: Understanding the DPI ecosystem requires navigating a complex landscape of organizations, standards, technologies, and governance models. This final module provides practical frameworks for decision-making, stakeholder engagement, and strategic planning in DPI development.

keyPoints.title: DPI Maturity Assessment Framework
keyPoints.description: A systematic approach to assess your country's DPI maturity across identity, payments, and data sharing. Identify current state, required improvements, and sequencing of investments.
keyPoints.example: Rwanda's DPI assessment identified that Huduma-like identity was the missing foundation. This led to prioritizing NIDA (National ID Authority) development before expanding payment systems and government data sharing.

keyPoints.title: Stakeholder Engagement Strategy
keyPoints.description: DPI requires alignment across government ministries, regulators, financial institutions, technology providers, and civil society. Effective engagement strategies address differing incentives and build consensus.
keyPoints.example: India's DPI success required coordination between UIDAI (Aadhaar authority), central bank (for digital payments regulation), NPCI (payment operator), and tax authority (GSTIN). Regular inter-agency committees resolved conflicts.

keyPoints.title: Governance and Institutional Design
keyPoints.description: DPI governance requires clarity on data ownership, liability, security standards, and dispute resolution. Institutional arrangements vary—from government ownership to independent authorities to public-private partnerships.
keyPoints.example: Estonia established the Information System Authority (RIA) as an independent agency managing X-Road and digital governance standards, insulating technical decisions from political cycles while maintaining government accountability.

keyPoints.title: Security and Privacy Framework
keyPoints.description: DPI security is foundational—breaches can undermine citizen trust in the entire ecosystem. Frameworks must address authentication security, data protection, encryption standards, and incident response.
keyPoints.example: India's Aadhaar faced initial security concerns about biometric privacy. This led to legislative protections (Aadhaar Act), technical improvements, and the development of consent-based data sharing frameworks that became best practice globally.

keyPoints.title: Regulatory and Policy Alignment
keyPoints.description: DPI requires regulatory clarity on data sharing, digital signatures, financial regulation, and platform governance. Policies should enable innovation while protecting citizens.
keyPoints.example: Brazil's Open Banking Regulation explicitly enabled banks to share customer data through standardized APIs, removing regulatory uncertainty and accelerating fintech innovation on the DPI foundation.

keyPoints.title: Measurement and Feedback
keyPoints.description: Establish metrics for DPI success: adoption rates, transaction volumes, service coverage, and user satisfaction. Create feedback mechanisms to improve system performance and identify gaps.
keyPoints.example: India tracks UPI adoption through transaction volumes (growing from 90 million to 8+ billion monthly) and user demographics, identifying gaps in underserved regions and driving targeted adoption programs.

content.keyInsight: Navigating the DPI ecosystem is a strategic, ongoing process, not a one-time implementation project. Success requires balancing technical excellence with governance clarity, stakeholder alignment, and user trust. Start with foundational components, establish clear governance, and expand systematically based on demonstrated success and capacity.

exercises.prompt: Develop a 3-year DPI strategy for your country or organization. Include: current state assessment, priority components, governance model, stakeholder engagement approach, and success metrics.

You're implementing DPI in a country facing significant institutional fragmentation, corruption concerns, and technical capacity constraints. Design a governance and implementation approach that addresses these challenges while building ecosystem trust.

You've been assigned to build partnerships for your country's DPI initiative. Identify which multilateral organizations, regional bodies, technical communities, and country peers you would engage, and develop a communication strategy for each stakeholder group.
